meta.title: Code Heroes — the programmers who build a hundred repos

hero.name: Code Heroes
hero.tagline: Programmers who build hundreds of repositories and make thousands of commits.
hero.lede: Code Heroes is a public list of programmers who have a hundred public repositories of their own, every one of them real code. The bar to join is ten. Ten public repositories put a name on the list; the count beside it runs to a hundred. Anyone can check an entry, and anyone can add one with a pull request.

items.name: 100 public repositories of your own
items.body: “Public” means that anyone can open, read, and clone the repository. “Your own” means that you created it. Forks of other people’s repositories do not count.

items.name: Each repository must contain real code
items.body: Each repository must have at least 10 commits and more than 100 lines of code in any programming language.

items.name: At least one repository with 1,000 commits
items.body: At least one of your public repositories must contain 1,000 or more commits.

heroes.title: Code Heroes
heroes.none: There is no hero of 100 applications yet!

join.title: Be a hero
join.lede: The list lives in a GitHub repository, and an entry is one pull request.

steps.name: One file
steps.body: Add data/heroes/<handle>.json: your name, your links, and at least ten applications, each with its public repository.

steps.name: Pull request
steps.body: Open a pull request. A check runs on it: the file parses, there are ten applications, every repository answers. The rest is read by a person.

join.language: The list is written in English. Where a description carries a translation, the page shows it in the reader's language.
join.collected: Not every entry is written by the person it names. The people who keep the site also collect entries themselves, and those are checked and corrected the same way as any other.
join.prompt: Or copy the prompt, give it to an AI assistant with a GitHub profile, and it writes the file.

check.title: Check yourself
check.lede: Put a GitHub username in and the rules are read against that account: every public repository of their own that is not a fork, how many commits it has, and how much code is in it. An organisation counts too, and several accounts separated by commas are read as one.
check.own: {{own}} public repositories of their own, {{all}} counting forks.
check.ownAcross: {{own}} public repositories of their own across {{accounts}} accounts, {{all}} counting forks.
check.none: nothing near a thousand commits yet
check.hero: A hero: a hundred repositories that count, and one of them with a thousand commits.
check.listed: On the list: {{n}} of the hundred. Ten is the bar to join.
check.under: {{n}} of the ten the list starts at.
check.sieve: The second rule is the sieve the first counts through: a repository counts when it is yours, not a fork, and has 10 commits or more and more than 100 lines of code. Lines are read off the bytes GitHub gives for each language, at thirty bytes a line, so a repository near the line is worth a second look.

why.prose: no code, only prose or data

check.notAName: That is not a GitHub username.
check.tooMany: At most {{n}} accounts at a time.
check.limit: Too many checks from here this hour. Try again later.
check.busy: Too many checks waiting just now. Try again in a minute.
check.github: GitHub would not answer. Try again in a moment.
check.off: The check is not answering. It runs beside the page; if this is a local copy, its server may be off.
check.failed: The check could not finish. Try again in a moment.
